nodes.name: Question: recover the resurgence structure from the new Borel transforms
nodes.statement: At this stage we are back to our main question. The Borel transforms computed in section~\ref{sec:quartic}, \eqref{borel-quartic-int} and \eqref{borel-quartic-int-inst}, had a singularity structure with poles and logarithms, \eqref{borel-quartic-int-expanded} and \eqref{borel-quartic-int-expanded-inst}, which immediately made explicit the resurgence properties of the quartic partition-function. In fact, the abstraction of these resurgence properties out from their associated Borel singularities, realized in the resurgence relations \eqref{Delta+A} and \eqref{Delta-A}, or in the (finite) alien chain \eqref{linear-algebraic-structure}, was what then allowed to jump-start the whole resurgence program. But will the same remain true with the Borel transforms we have just computed, \eqref{eq:Borel-Z0-after-change-var} and \eqref{eq:Borel-Z1-after-change-var}? How can we recover the (algebraic) resurgence structure encoded in \eqref{linear-algebraic-structure} out of these ``new'' Borel transforms?
nodes.statement_short: Question: recover the resurgence structure from the new Borel transforms
nodes.section: Constructing Borel Transforms: Some Examples

nodes.name: Focus on the singularities at $s=\pm A$
nodes.statement: The first thing to notice is that the Borel transforms \eqref{eq:Borel-Z0-after-change-var} and \eqref{eq:Borel-Z1-after-change-var} both have a square-root singularity at the origin, \textit{i.e.}, $\sim 1/\sqrt{s}$ near $s=0$. This is a somewhat artificial singularity from the resurgence standpoint, and is essentially related to the coupling square-root in the initial asymptotic expansion. In order to infer whether there is any clean resurgent behaviour in our ``new'' Borel transforms, we need to analyze them away from this singularity. In fact, we shall need to focus on the singularity at $s=\frac{3}{2}$ of the Borel transform ${\cal B}[\Psi_0](s)$, and on the singularity at $s=-\frac{3}{2}$ of the Borel transform ${\cal B}[\Psi_1](s)$. If resurgence is also at work in here, near each of these singularities we should see the ``reappearance'' of the other sector.
nodes.statement_short: Focus on the singularities at $s=\pm A$
nodes.section: Constructing Borel Transforms: Some Examples

nodes.name: Expand both Borel transforms near their singularities
nodes.statement: Expanding the Borel transforms \eqref{eq:Borel-Z0-after-change-var} and \eqref{eq:Borel-Z1-after-change-var} near their singularities at $s = \pm A \equiv \pm \frac{3}{2}$, we find \begin{eqnarray} {\cal B}[\Psi_0](s) &=& \sum_{k=-1}^{+\infty} B_k^{(0)} \left( s - A \right)^{\frac{k}{2}}, \qquad B_k^{(0)} = \frac{{\mathrm{e}}^{{\mathrm{i}} \frac{k\pi}{2}}}{2\pi^{3/2}}\, \frac{\Gamma \left( k+\frac{3}{2} \right)}{\Gamma \left( k+2 \right)}\, A^{-\frac{k+1}{2}}, \\ {\cal B}[\Psi_1](s) &=& \sum_{k=-1}^{+\infty} B_k^{(1)} \left( s + A \right)^{\frac{k}{2}}, \qquad B_k^{(1)} = \frac{{\mathrm{e}}^{{\mathrm{i}}\pi}}{\left(2\pi\right)^{3/2}}\, \frac{\Gamma \left( k+\frac{3}{2} \right)}{\Gamma \left( k+2 \right)}\, A^{-\frac{k+1}{2}}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Expand both Borel transforms near their singularities
nodes.section: Constructing Borel Transforms: Some Examples

nodes.name: Match singular coefficients with the shifted instanton Borel transform
nodes.statement: Recall that back in \eqref{borel-quartic-int-expanded} and \eqref{borel-quartic-int-expanded-inst} the singularities were restricted to a simple pole and a logarithm branch-cut. Things here are a bit ``messier'', as there is now an \textit{infinite number} of branch-cuts, one per fractional power in the above expansions (\textit{i.e.}, whenever $k$ is odd). Thus, at first sight, it now seems much harder to find the resurgence of, say, the $\Psi_1$ sector inside the expansion of ${\cal B}[\Psi_0](s)$ around $s=A$, due to this plethora of branch-cuts. This scenario quickly becomes more amenable once one computes the expansion of ${\cal B}[\Psi_1](s-A)$ near $s=A$ (which anyways is what we hope to find inside ${\cal B}[\Psi_0](s)$ near $s=A$ in the first place). One easily obtains \begin{equation} {\cal B}[\Psi_1] \left(s-A\right) = \sum_{k=-1}^{+\infty} \widehat{B}_k^{(1)} \left( s - A \right)^{k+\frac{1}{2}}, \qquad \widehat{B}_k^{(1)} = \frac{{\mathrm{i}}\, {\mathrm{e}}^{{\mathrm{i}}\pi k}}{2\pi^{3/2}}\, \frac{\Gamma \left( 2k+\frac{5}{2} \right)}{\Gamma \left( 2k+3 \right)}\, A^{- \left( k+1 \right)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Match singular coefficients with the shifted instanton Borel transform
nodes.section: Constructing Borel Transforms: Some Examples

nodes.name: Resurgence-like relation for $\mathcal{B}[\Psi_0]$
nodes.statement: Comparing the coefficients $\widehat{B}_k^{(1)}$ with those particular coefficients $B_k^{(0)}$ which were attached to a \textit{singular} fractional-power, \textit{i.e.}, with the coefficients $B_{2k+1}^{(0)}$, one finds \begin{equation} B_{2k+1}^{(0)} = \widehat{B}_k^{(1)}. \end{equation} \noindent In this way, one may \textit{split} the power-series expansion \eqref{expansion-Borel-sqrt} into its regular \textit{holomorphic} half and its \textit{singular} half, both of which are \textit{infinite series} on their own. Then, the singular series will match \eqref{psi1borelHAT} above in such a way that one can write the resurgence-like relation \begin{equation} {\cal B}[\Psi_0](s) = \left( + 2 \right) \times \frac{1}{2}\, {\cal B}[\Psi_1] \left(s-A\right) + \text{holomorphic}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Resurgence-like relation for $\mathcal{B}[\Psi_0]$
nodes.section: Constructing Borel Transforms: Some Examples

nodes.name: Same analysis for $\mathcal{B}[\Psi_1]$
nodes.statement: The exact same analysis equally applies to ${\cal B}[\Psi_1](s)$. This time around \begin{equation} {\cal B}[\Psi_0] \left(s+A\right) = \sum_{k=-1}^{+\infty} \widehat{B}_k^{(0)} \left( s + A \right)^{k+\frac{1}{2}}, \qquad \widehat{B}_k^{(0)} = \frac{1}{2^{1/2}\pi^{3/2}}\, \frac{\Gamma \left( 2k+\frac{5}{2} \right)}{\Gamma \left( 2k+3 \right)}\, A^{- \left( k+1 \right)}, \end{equation} \noindent in such a way that \begin{equation} B_{2k+1}^{(1)} = - \frac{1}{2}\, \widehat{B}_k^{(0)}, \end{equation} \noindent from where the resurgence-like relation emerges \begin{equation} {\cal B}[\Psi_1](s) = \left( - 1 \right) \times \frac{1}{2}\, {\cal B}[\Psi_0] \left(s+A\right) + \text{holomorphic}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Same analysis for $\mathcal{B}[\Psi_1]$
nodes.section: Constructing Borel Transforms: Some Examples

nodes.name: Read off the Stokes constants via the odd-$d$ dictionary
nodes.statement: One may compare these results, \eqref{resurgentPsi0} and \eqref{resurgentPsi1}, to \eqref{borel-quartic-int-expanded} and \eqref{borel-quartic-int-expanded-inst}, respectively. Recall that one needs to use the ``dictionary'' from \eqref{eq:B_Psi_n:d=odd} to read Stokes constants. In this way, via \eqref{eq:B_Psi_n:d=odd}, \eqref{resurgentPsi0} yields the Stokes constant $S_1 = - 2$, which is the precise constant obtained in \eqref{Delta+A}. Likewise, \eqref{resurgentPsi1} yields the Stokes constant $S_{-1} = 1$, which matches the one obtained in \eqref{Delta-A}.
nodes.statement_short: Read off the Stokes constants via the odd-$d$ dictionary
nodes.section: Constructing Borel Transforms: Some Examples

nodes.name: A proof is still owed and is simple
nodes.statement: We have mentioned Stokes phenomenon in the one-dimensional setting, \eqref{stokespheno}, but we are still short of a proof for such statement (another simple proof, based on the bridge equations, may be found in appendix~\ref{app:alien-calculus}). This is actually very simple, in light of the combinatorics of the Borel residues.
nodes.statement_short: A proof is still owed and is simple
nodes.section: Stokes Discontinuities and Transseries Asymptotics

nodes.name: Transseries and binomial Borel residues
nodes.statement: Consider the one-dimensional setting with transseries \eqref{Phitransseries} and \eqref{Phi(n)}, \begin{equation} \Phi (x,\sigma) = \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} \sigma^n\, {\mathrm{e}}^{-n \frac{A}{x}}\, \Phi_n (x), \end{equation} \noindent and forward ($\theta=0$) Stokes automorphism \eqref{one-param-stokes-0}, or, equivalently for our present purposes, forward Borel residues \eqref{stokesS-to-borelS+GEN}---which we shall now write binomially as \begin{equation} \mathsf{S}_{n\to n+\ell} = - \binom{n+\ell}{\ell}\, S_1^\ell. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Transseries and binomial Borel residues
nodes.section: Stokes Discontinuities and Transseries Asymptotics

nodes.name: Resum the Stokes automorphism on the full transseries
nodes.statement: Instead of focusing solely on the action of the Stokes automorphism upon a transseries \textit{node}, as we have been doing up to now, we may ask what is the action of the Stokes automorphism on the \textit{full transseries}. The calculation is elementary, but illustrative: \begin{eqnarray} \underline{\mathfrak{S}}_0 \Phi (x,\sigma) &=& \Phi (x,\sigma) - \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} \sigma^n\, {\mathrm{e}}^{-n \frac{A}{x}}\, {\mathrm{Disc}}_0 \Phi_n (x) = - \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} \sum_{\ell=0}^{+\infty} \mathsf{S}_{n\to n+\ell}\, \sigma^n\, {\mathrm{e}}^{- \left( n+\ell \right) \frac{A}{x}}\, \Phi_{n+\ell} \\ && \hspace{-30pt} = \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} \sum_{\ell=0}^{+\infty} \binom{n+\ell}{\ell}\, S_1^\ell\, \sigma^n\, {\mathrm{e}}^{- \left( n+\ell \right) \frac{A}{x}}\, \Phi_{n+\ell} = \sum_{m=0}^{+\infty} \left( \sigma+S_1 \right)^m {\mathrm{e}}^{-m \frac{A}{x}}\, \Phi_m (x) = \Phi \left( x,\sigma+S_1 \right), \nonumber \end{eqnarray} \noindent where the key step occurs at the beginning of the second line, when we make use of the binomial formulation \eqref{stokesS-to-borelS+GEN-BINOMIAL}.
nodes.statement_short: Resum the Stokes automorphism on the full transseries
nodes.section: Stokes Discontinuities and Transseries Asymptotics

nodes.name: Parallel Stokes vectors make the algebra close
nodes.statement: The other simple exercise to discuss is one of the cleanest scenarios where \eqref{closure-condition-stokes} is indeed verified and the alien-lattice algebra \eqref{eq:sec5-commutator-general-op-with stokes} \textit{closes}: this is the case where \textit{all} Stokes vectors are \textit{parallel}.
nodes.statement_short: Parallel Stokes vectors make the algebra close
nodes.section: Algebras of Alien Derivatives and Virasoro-Like Algebras

nodes.name: Choose a common direction $u$
nodes.statement: Let us pick some direction, defined by the versor $\boldsymbol{u}$, and let us suppose that all Stokes vectors, $\boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{n}}$, $\boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{m}}$, and $\boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{m}+\boldsymbol{n}}$, are parallel, \textit{i.e.}, \begin{equation} \boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{n}} \parallel \boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{m}} \parallel \boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{m}+\boldsymbol{n}} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \begin{cases} \,\, \boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{n}} = S_{\boldsymbol{n}}\, \boldsymbol{u}, \\ \,\, \boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{m}} = S_{\boldsymbol{m}}\, \boldsymbol{u}, \\ \,\, \boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{m}+\boldsymbol{n}} = S_{\boldsymbol{m}+\boldsymbol{n}}\, \boldsymbol{u}. \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Choose a common direction $u$
nodes.section: Algebras of Alien Derivatives and Virasoro-Like Algebras

nodes.name: Compute the closure combination and commutator
nodes.statement: This immediately implies that, in this case, \begin{equation} \left( \boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{n}} \cdot \boldsymbol{m} \right) \boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{m}} - \left( \boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{m}} \cdot \boldsymbol{n} \right) \boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{n}} = \boldsymbol{u} \cdot \left( \boldsymbol{m} - \boldsymbol{n} \right)\, S_{\boldsymbol{n}} S_{\boldsymbol{m}}\, \boldsymbol{u}, \end{equation} \noindent and thus the alien-lattice algebra \textit{closes} as \begin{equation} \left[ \frac{G_{\boldsymbol{n}} (\boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{n}})}{S_{\boldsymbol{n}}}, \frac{G_{\boldsymbol{m}} (\boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{m}})}{S_{\boldsymbol{m}}} \right] = \boldsymbol{u} \cdot \left( \boldsymbol{m} - \boldsymbol{n} \right) \frac{G_{\boldsymbol{m}+\boldsymbol{n}} (\boldsymbol{S}_{\boldsymbol{m}+\boldsymbol{n}})}{S_{\boldsymbol{m}+\boldsymbol{n}}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Compute the closure combination and commutator
nodes.section: Algebras of Alien Derivatives and Virasoro-Like Algebras

nodes.name: Same as the one-dimensional Virasoro-like result
nodes.statement: This is essentially the same result as in \eqref{1dALIENisVIR?}.
nodes.statement_short: Same as the one-dimensional Virasoro-like result
nodes.section: Algebras of Alien Derivatives and Virasoro-Like Algebras

nodes.name: The bridge equation follows from a simple observation
nodes.statement: The construction of the bridge equation now follows from a simple observation.
nodes.statement_short: The bridge equation follows from a simple observation
nodes.section: Transseries and the Bridge Equation

nodes.name: Pointed alien derivative commutes with $\partial_z$
nodes.statement: The \textit{pointed} alien derivative which we introduced earlier, $\dot{\Delta}_\omega$, turns out to commute with the \textit{ordinary} derivative, \textit{i.e.}, $[ \dot{\Delta}_\omega, \partial_z ] = 0$ (in particular, this implies that the \textit{standard} alien derivative $\Delta_\omega$ does \textit{not} commute with the ordinary derivative), see, \textit{e.g.}, \cite{e81, s07, s14}.
nodes.statement_short: Pointed alien derivative commutes with $\partial_z$
nodes.section: Transseries and the Bridge Equation

nodes.name: Same linear ODE implies proportionality
nodes.statement: Further, a partial derivative with respect to the transseries parameter, $\partial_\sigma$, obviously also commutes with $\partial_z$. This implies that both $\dot{\Delta}_\omega \Phi (z,\sigma)$ and $\partial_\sigma \Phi (z,\sigma)$ will satisfy the very \textit{same}, first-order ODE. In particular, this will be a \textit{linear}, homogeneous ODE in the variable $z$, which implies that these two quantities must be \textit{proportional} to each other.
nodes.statement_short: Same linear ODE implies proportionality
nodes.section: Transseries and the Bridge Equation

nodes.name: Goal: derive the relation within a resurgence class
nodes.statement: This appendix presents a formal derivation of the relation between Borel transforms within the same resurgence class; equation \eqref{eq:finding-Borel-rep-from-other} in the main text.
nodes.statement_short: Goal: derive the relation within a resurgence class
nodes.section: E Further Details on Borel Transforms

nodes.name: Family $\Phi_{[\gamma]}$ and its truncated Borel transforms
nodes.statement: Let us consider a family of asymptotic series in the same resurgence class---with the class specified by the constants $\alpha$ and $\beta$ (different sets yielding different classes) and the family $\{ \Phi_{[\gamma]} \}$ parameterized by $\gamma$---which is given by \begin{equation} \Phi_{[\gamma]} (\lambda) = \lambda^\gamma\, \Phi_{[0]} (\lambda) \simeq \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} \Phi_k\, \lambda^{\alpha k + \beta + \gamma}, \end{equation} \noindent and where we are taking $\Phi_{[0]}$ to be the standard representative. This essentially means that the coefficients $\Phi_k$ have the precise (large-order) factorial growth of \begin{equation} \Phi_k \sim \left( \alpha k + \beta - 1 \right)!, \end{equation} \noindent and that the Borel transform ${\cal B} [\Phi_{[0]}] (s)$ will have the singular structure \eqref{simpleBorelsingularities}. All other Borel transforms, associated with each other element in this family of functions, will be defined as \begin{equation} {\cal B} [ \widehat{\Phi}_{[\gamma]} ] (s) = \sum_{k=n_0(\gamma)}^{+\infty} \Phi_k\, \frac{s^{\alpha k + \beta + \gamma - 1}}{\Gamma \left( \alpha k + \beta + \gamma \right)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Family $\Phi_{[\gamma]}$ and its truncated Borel transforms
nodes.section: E Further Details on Borel Transforms

nodes.name: Truncation of leading terms
nodes.statement: Let us explain the notation. In order to obtain the Borel transform of the generic element $\Phi_{[\gamma]} (\lambda)$, one first needs to remove the first $k<n_{0}(\gamma)$ terms within its asymptotic expansion, in such a way that $\alpha\, n_{0}(\gamma)+\beta+\gamma>0$ and the Borel transform is thus well-defined. This ``truncated'' asymptotic series is then denoted by $\widehat{\Phi}_{[\gamma]} (\lambda)$. As to the terms which get removed, they are handled separately, and can be added back-in at the very end, once we have Borel resummed and obtained ${\cal S}_\theta \widehat{\Phi}_{[\gamma]}$ following the standard procedures. In order to simplify our present discussion, we will not consider these terms as they are always straightforward to add at any stage.
nodes.statement_short: Truncation of leading terms
nodes.section: E Further Details on Borel Transforms

nodes.name: Integer shifts: derivatives and primitives
nodes.statement: For integer values of $\gamma$, the straightforward relation (with $n,m \in {\mathbb N}^+$) \begin{equation} \frac{s^n}{\Gamma \left( n+1 \right)} = \frac{{\mathrm{d}}^m}{{\mathrm{d}} s^m}\, \frac{s^{n+m}}{\Gamma \left( n+m+1 \right)} \end{equation} \noindent directly implies the relation between Borel transforms\footnote{As an historical aside, note that this sort of relations was probably first noticed in \cite{bpv78b}, but, unfortunately, the role of the standard representative---with its (simple) logarithmic ramified structure, and where resurgent analysis becomes most straightforward---was not emphasized enough to spark subsequent further analysis.} \begin{equation} {\cal B} [ \widehat{\Phi}_{[\gamma']} ] (s) = D_s^{\gamma-\gamma'} {\cal B} [ \widehat{\Phi}_{[\gamma]} ] (s). \end{equation} \noindent Assuming that $\gamma-\gamma'$ is an integer and that $\gamma>\gamma'$, the operator $D_s^n$ is herein defined as the $n$th derivative with respect to $s$. The relation \eqref{eq:relation-between-borels-der} also holds if $\gamma<\gamma'$, in which case one simply defines $D_s^n$ as the $n$th \textit{primitive}\footnote{Each primitive yields an integration constant, and upon multiple primitivation one obtains a polynomial in $s$ with maximum degree $\gamma'-\gamma$. This polynomial is directly related to the first $n_0(\gamma)$ coefficients which were removed from the original asymptotic series $\Phi_{[\gamma]} (\lambda)$ in order to obtain the ``Borel transformable'' asymptotic series $\widehat{\Phi}_{[\gamma]} (\lambda)$.} with respect to $s$. If $\gamma=\gamma'$ then $D_s^0$ is simply the identity.
nodes.statement_short: Integer shifts: derivatives and primitives
nodes.section: E Further Details on Borel Transforms

nodes.name: Real shifts: fractional derivative
nodes.statement: The assumption that $\gamma-\gamma'$ is an integer may be lifted, allowing \eqref{eq:relation-between-borels-der} to be valid for a \textit{continuous} parameter $\gamma \in {\mathbb R}$. Let us show how this is done when\footnote{The case where $\gamma<\gamma'$ follows in complete analogy by simply inverting \eqref{eq:relation-between-borels-der} and having the operator $D_s^{\gamma'-\gamma}$, which is now a \textit{derivative}, acting on ${\cal B} [ \widehat{\Phi}_{[\gamma']} ] (s)$.} $\gamma>\gamma'$. In this case we have to deal with a \textit{fractional derivative}, where $D_s^\alpha$ is defined, when $0<\alpha<1$, as (see, \textit{e.g.}, \cite{lot76}) \begin{equation} D_s^\alpha f(s) = \frac{1}{\Gamma \left(1-\alpha\right)}\, \frac{{\mathrm{d}}}{{\mathrm{d}} s} \int_0^s {\mathrm{d}} t\, \frac{f(t)}{\left( s-t \right)^{\alpha}}. \end{equation} \noindent This definition naturally extends to any real order $\gamma$ by setting $\gamma = \alpha + m$, with $\gamma \in {\mathbb R}$, $m \in {\mathbb N}_+$, and $\alpha$ as above, in which case \begin{equation} D_s^\gamma f(s) = D_s^\alpha D_s^m f(s) = D_s^\alpha\, \frac{{\mathrm{d}}^m f}{{\mathrm{d}} s^m} (s). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Real shifts: fractional derivative
nodes.section: E Further Details on Borel Transforms

nodes.name: Apply the fractional derivative term by term
nodes.statement: Applying the fractional derivative to each term in the definition of a Borel transform is straightforward; one only needs to know that, for $f(s) = s^\rho$, $\rho>-1$, one has \begin{equation} D_s^\alpha s^\rho = \frac{\Gamma \left(\rho+1\right)}{\Gamma \left(\rho+1-\alpha\right)}\, s^{\rho-\alpha}. \end{equation} \noindent The action of the fractional derivative $D_s^{\gamma-\gamma'}$ on the Borel transform ${\cal B} [ \widehat{\Phi}_{[\gamma]} ] (s)$ in \eqref{eq:relation-between-borels-der} can then be easily computed making use of the above expression order-by-order in the series definition of ${\cal B} [ \widehat{\Phi}_{[\gamma]} ] (s)$. One obtains \begin{equation} D_s^{\gamma-\gamma'} {\cal B} [ \widehat{\Phi}_{[\gamma]} ] (s) = \sum_{k=n_0(\gamma)}^{+\infty} \Phi_k\, \frac{s^{\alpha k + \beta + \gamma' - 1}}{\Gamma \left( \alpha k + \beta + \gamma' \right)} \approx {\cal B} [ \widehat{\Phi}_{[\gamma']} ] (s). \end{equation} \noindent We have used the symbol $\approx$ as a reminder that this equality only holds up to the removal/addition of $\gamma-\gamma'$ initial terms in the expansions (residual coefficients \textit{et al}).
nodes.statement_short: Apply the fractional derivative term by term
nodes.section: E Further Details on Borel Transforms

nodes.name: Perturbative node is consistent with the one-parameter chain
nodes.statement: Take a closer look at the first two sectors in the transseries; the $\Phi_0$ and $\Phi_1$ nodes in the chain. As shown in figure~\ref{fig:Pade-poles-quartic-pert-series}, the Borel transform of the perturbative sector has a branch-cut starting at $s=A$. Figure~\ref{fig:first-5-sector-alien-1-param} then shows how this is correctly reproduced by our transseries \textit{ansatz}: there are no singularities along the negative real axis because $\Phi_0$ is the first node in the chain, and there is indeed one singularity at $s=A$ because $\Delta_A \Phi_0 \propto \Phi_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Perturbative node is consistent with the one-parameter chain
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis

nodes.name: One-instanton sector shows a cut at $s=-A$
nodes.statement: But figure~\ref{fig:Pade-poles-quartic-pert-series} also illustrates how the one-instanton sector has \textit{two} branch-cuts, one similarly starting at $s=A$, but another at $s=-A$ along the \textit{negative} real axis.
nodes.statement_short: One-instanton sector shows a cut at $s=-A$
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis

nodes.name: Contradiction with $\Delta_{-A}\Phi_1=0$
nodes.statement: As is made very clear in figure~\ref{fig:first-5-sector-alien-1-param}, this \textit{cannot} happen within the one-parameter transseries set-up: in this case there should be a single singularity at $s=A$ and none at $s=-A$, because $\Delta_{-A}\Phi_1=0$ (\textit{i.e.}, one has $\mathsf{S}_{1\to0}=0$)!
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction with $\Delta_{-A}\Phi_1=0$
nodes.section: 2.4 First Steps Towards Nonlinear Resurgent Analysis

nodes.name: Use the large-order relation
nodes.statement: This can also be seen from the large-order behaviour of the perturbative coefficients in \eqref{large_order_aA} (and illustrated in figure~\ref{fig:large_order-res}).
nodes.statement_short: Use the large-order relation
nodes.section: 6.8 Linear Resonant-Asymptotics: Partition Function

nodes.name: Recall the modular relation between instanton coefficients
nodes.statement: Recall that, due to the modular symmetry \eqref{modular_sym}, the coefficients in the partition-function nonperturbative sectors relate to each other as $Z^{(2)}_n (m) = (-1)^n\, Z^{(1)}_n(m^\prime)$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the modular relation between instanton coefficients
nodes.section: 6.8 Linear Resonant-Asymptotics: Partition Function

nodes.name: Odd terms cancel at $m=1/2$
nodes.statement: Thus, for $m=m^\prime=\frac{1}{2}$ and consequentially $A_1 = -A_2$, one can immediately see that all the odd $n$ terms cancel in \eqref{large_order_aA}.
nodes.statement_short: Odd terms cancel at $m=1/2$
nodes.section: 6.8 Linear Resonant-Asymptotics: Partition Function

nodes.name: Destructive interference of the two saddles
nodes.statement: This phenomenon is a straightforward consequence of the fact that both nonperturbative saddles contribute to the large-order growth of the perturbative series with the \textit{same} magnitude but with \textit{symmetric} values (\textit{i.e.}, the contribution of saddle $(2)$ is alternating while that of saddle $(1)$ is not). This leads to the ``destructive interference'' which causes all odd terms in the perturbative series to vanish.
nodes.statement_short: Destructive interference of the two saddles
nodes.section: 6.8 Linear Resonant-Asymptotics: Partition Function

nodes.name: Assign weights to transmonomials
nodes.statement: One may be more specific about the proportionality coefficient $S_\omega(\sigma)$. The transmonomial building blocks of \eqref{Phitransseries-app} are of the form $\sigma^n {\mathrm{e}}^{m A z}$, to which we may assign weight $\mathsf{w} = n+m$.
nodes.statement_short: Assign weights to transmonomials
nodes.section: Transseries and the Bridge Equation

nodes.name: Weight-lowering action of the two derivatives
nodes.statement: Now, the derivative $\dot{\Delta}_{k A}$ acts on these transmonomials by lowering\footnote{For positive $k$ and $A$, which is implicitly assumed when saying ``lowering''.} their weight as $m \to m-k$ and the derivative $\partial_\sigma$ acts upon them by lowering weight as $n \to n-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Weight-lowering action of the two derivatives
nodes.section: Transseries and the Bridge Equation

nodes.name: Homogeneity forces a monomial coefficient
nodes.statement: Since the transseries \eqref{Phitransseries-app} has overall weight $\mathsf{w}=0$, the bridge equation \eqref{bridge-equation-app} can only hold\footnote{These concepts of degree and homogeneity were further discussed, in a slightly different context, in section~\ref{sec:physics}.} at $\omega = k A$ if $S_{k A} (\sigma)$ has weight $\mathsf{w} = 1-k$, \textit{i.e.}, \begin{equation} S_{k A} (\sigma) \equiv S_k\, \sigma^{1-k} \end{equation} \noindent is a monomial in $\sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Homogeneity forces a monomial coefficient
nodes.section: Transseries and the Bridge Equation
